species.identification: A day-flying castniid moth. Males have a wingspan of about 34 mm, dark brown forewings with pale grey marks, and bronze-brown hindwings. Females are about 31 mm, with bright orange hindwings and black submarginal spots, and they rarely fly. Adults have clubbed antennae, green eyes and no working mouthparts. Empty red-brown pupal cases stick out of the soil near grass tussocks. It is not a sun-moth you should expect on an ordinary walk: local evidence is three Victorian Biodiversity Atlas rows, all dated 2009, at about -38.0106, 144.057, inside 10 km and outside 5 km. Two coordinates differ only in the fifth decimal of longitude. iNaturalist has no observation within 10 km.
species.season: The national recovery plan says adults fly on warm dry days from mid-October to early January, usually for six to eight weeks, and live only one to four days. Victorian iNaturalist records (151) are mostly November and December. The Inverleigh-area rows are all from 2009, so they do not show a recent flight.
species.hostPlants: Larvae eat roots of wallaby grasses (Rytidosperma, formerly Austrodanthonia) and spear grasses (Austrostipa), and the moth also breeds in degraded grassland dominated by Chilean needle-grass (Nassella neesiana) and serrated tussock (Nassella trichotoma). Adults do not feed. The Inverleigh reserve's ground layer is described as dominated by wallaby grass, which is the right kind of habitat, but that does not prove the moth is still there.
species.whereToSeeLocally: Low, open native grassland, not the shaded interior of woodland. The 2009 points lie about 10 km north of the -38.10, 144.05 search centre. There is no 5 km record. Surveys, if done, belong in the flying season and should follow the recovery plan rather than general butterfly methods.
species.safety: No sting and no functional mouth. The conservation issue is trampling and collection, not a bite.
species.conservation: Vulnerable under the EPBC Act. It was listed as Critically Endangered in 2002 and reassessed as Vulnerable in 2021 after more survey increased the known area of occupancy; the national recovery plan, made with Victoria and the ACT, took effect on 10 June 2026. The July 2026 FFG Threatened List lists Synemon plana as Vulnerable, with extinction risk given as Australia. ALA conservation statuses on this access: Australia Vulnerable, Victoria Vulnerable, NSW Vulnerable, ACT Vulnerable. It is the only insect in the local ALA threatened-species facets.

species.identification: A black Myrmecia with orange to yellow jaws and legs, about 10–15 mm, that moves in short jumps. Workers are about 12–14 mm and queens about 14–16 mm. It is the ant most often named in Australian ant-sting allergy. ASCIA treats jack jumpers as a group of Myrmecia about 10–15 mm long, and bulldog ants as the larger species about 15–25 mm. iNaturalist also has a pilosula-group complex, so some similar ants may be filed there instead of under this species.
species.season: Across Victoria, iNaturalist records (2688 observations, place id 7830) fall mostly in March, September, October, November, December. Very few fall in June, July. Counts mix adults and younger stages and follow when people are outside, so they are not an Inverleigh flight calendar. Workers are active mainly by day and are recorded through the warmer months, with fewer records in winter.
species.hostPlants: They hunt small insects and kill them with a barbless sting. They are not plant-eaters. Nests are in bushland, woodland and dry open forest, often in gravel and sand.
species.whereToSeeLocally: Open sandy or gravelly ground in the reserve and rural blocks. Recorded inside 5 km. Other dangerous Myrmecia are also in the extracts: black-scaped bull ant inside 5 km, and inch ant, tawny-legged jack jumper and black-headed bull ant mostly in the 10 km circle. Any large jumping or bull ant should be treated as this kind of risk.
species.safety: The sting is very painful. Local swelling is common. In areas where jack jumpers live, about 2–3% of people have had a generalised allergic reaction, and deaths from anaphylaxis have occurred in Australia. About 70% of people with the allergy react again if stung. Signs of anaphylaxis include breathing difficulty, tongue or throat swelling, widespread hives, dizziness or collapse, and a pale floppy child. Those signs need emergency care. Venom immunotherapy exists, including at Monash Hospital in Melbourne. Do not disturb nests.

notWellDocumented: The local 5 km records were not re-checked against the pilosula species complex, so some may be look-alike jack jumpers.
Which other Myrmecia at Inverleigh have caused allergy locally was not studied. A 2011 Australian study found bulldog ants as well as jack jumpers among anaphylaxis cases.

species.identification: The redback. The Australian Faunal Directory and ALA accept Latrodectus hasseltii Thorell, 1870. iNaturalist uses Latrodectus hasselti and counted 2 observations within 10 km and none within 5 km. ALA counted 2 under hasseltii within 10 km and none within 5 km. Those are parallel spellings, not four spiders, and they still should not be added to each other because ALA ingests iNaturalist. The adult female is about 1 cm, glossy black, with a red or orange stripe on the abdomen and a red hourglass underneath. Males are about 3–4 mm and are not the dangerous sex. The web is a messy tangle in dry shelter.
species.season: Across Victoria, iNaturalist records (1634 observations, place id 7830) fall mostly in January, February, March, April, October. No month is below 1.5 percent of that Victorian total, so the histogram does not mark a closed season. Counts mix adults and younger stages and follow when people are outside, so they are not an Inverleigh flight calendar. The histogram uses the iNaturalist spelling. Records occur year-round. The Museum says bites are most often reported in summer. Males sit at the edge of a female's web in the summer mating season.
species.hostPlants: They eat insects and sometimes larger animals caught in the web, including other spiders, king crickets and small lizards. They are not plant-eaters.
species.whereToSeeLocally: Dry sheltered spots around buildings: meter boxes, the underside of outdoor furniture, stored shoes, sheds and cubbies. The RCH says they rarely leave the web, so bites happen when someone puts a hand into the web. No record inside 5 km in either spelling; two within 10 km.
species.safety: Only the female bite is dangerous. The Museum says bites can cause serious illness and that deaths have occurred, and that many people receive antivenom. The Royal Children's Hospital says she is the major medically significant spider in Victoria and is very unlikely to cause life-threatening envenomation. species.identification: A large golden orb-weaver, formerly placed in Nephila, family Nephilidae. Females are the large web spiders; the golden silk is the field mark. totals.method: Counts come from docs/research/data/insects.json, which stores the ALA species facet and the iNaturalist species_counts response for class Insecta or Arachnida (iNaturalist iconic_taxa Insecta,Arachnida) around -38.10, 144.05. ALA returned 192 binomials within 5 km and 344 within 10 km. Every name has two words, and every 5 km name is also in the 10 km facet. Both totals are below the facet limit of 500, so the species facet does not look truncated. iNaturalist page 1 (per_page 500) returned 218 taxa within 5 km, of which 160 are rank species, and 365 taxa within 10 km, of which 251 are rank species. Both are below 500, so a second page is not required. ALA largely ingests iNaturalist, so record counts were never added. Distinct species is the union of ALA binomials and iNaturalist names of rank species: 201 within 5 km (151 shared, 41 ALA-only, 9 iNaturalist-only) and 358 within 10 km (237 shared, 107 ALA-only, 14 iNaturalist-only). Genera, families and other ranks are excluded. Latrodectus hasseltii (ALA, 10 km only) and Latrodectus hasselti (iNaturalist, 10 km only) are one species under two spellings, so a spelling-collapsed 10 km total would be 357. The 5 km total is unchanged because neither spelling is inside 5 km. No cicada species, and no genus Psaltoda, Yoyetta, Galanga or family Cicadidae, is in the file or in live ALA or iNaturalist queries within 10 km. Galanga (iNaturalist taxon 473988, preferred common name Double-spotted Cicadas) is a cicada genus in family Cicadidae. The English Wikipedia summary describes it as monotypic, named by Moulds in 2012, with its single species in subtropical and warm temperate eastern Australia. ALA genus searches at 5 km and 10 km, and iNaturalist species counts for taxon 473988 at both radii, returned zero, so no cicada from this genus is in the local extract. A search result pointed at an Australian Faunal Directory genus page; a direct request returned HTTP 404, so that page was not used for a state list. Perala viridis is in the file (4 records at both radii) under the iNaturalist common name Spring Buzzer, but ALA, iNaturalist and Catalogue of Life place it in the grasshopper family Acrididae, so it is not treated as a cicada. Native bees identified to species are Lasioglossum lanarium and Lipotriches australica inside 5 km, and Megachile ferox inside 10 km only. Hyleoides concinna, the common wasp-mimic bee, has one iNaturalist record inside 10 km and no ALA species count. Amegilla is one genus-only record. Homalictus is one subgenus-only record. Exoneura returned none. The only threatened insect in the local threatened-occurrence facets is the golden sun moth.
